name: Grace Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a nine-person branding agency, and almost all our clients make food or drink: two craft breweries, a sourdough bakery, a cheese maker, that sort of thing. A typical day is packaging, so beer can labels, box designs, little shelf signs. In the morning I'm usually on the computer, and once a week I go to the label printer to check colours on the press.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the press checks, honestly. Standing next to a huge machine with a cup of bad coffee, holding a wet label up to the light, is the best bit of the job. What drains me is the deadline crunch before a brewery launches a seasonal beer, when Marcus, the owner, promises them everything by Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit smugly. At work I'd say the tools are handy for boring jobs and nothing more. Online I'd probably share something about how human craft won, and then feel slightly embarrassed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd mean my job looks safe. I already use an image tool now and then to extend a photo background or mock up a can, and that saves me maybe an hour a week. The bigger worries would be the usual ones: breweries going bust, and Marcus overpromising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes. I'd keep using the tools for mock-ups, keep my eight months of savings where they are, and keep going to the press checks. I'd probably put more into my pension, since the scary future I'd been half-saving for didn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved and a bit flat, like when a storm warning turns out to be a light shower. It's good news, but you'd built yourself up for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned breweries going bust. How real is that worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly real. One of our brewery clients closed last spring and owed us for two months of work, and Marcus had to cut everyone's bonus. That kind of thing happens whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in the agency would you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena, our copywriter, because writing short product text is exactly the routine stuff these tools are decent at. Even in the hype picture, a client might write their own beer descriptions with a chatbot. She'd lose a slice of work before I would.

say: The AI tools are **handy for boring jobs** and nothing more.
**Human craft** won this round, and I'd say it a bit smugly.
think: My job looks **safe**; the image tool saves me about **an hour** a week.
The real worries stay **brewery clients** going bust and Marcus overpromising.
do: Keep using the image tool for **can mock-ups** and keep doing press checks.
Put **more into my pension**, since the scary future never came.
feel: **Relieved** and a little flat, like a storm warning that brings only light rain.
S0.quote: Even in the hype picture, a client might write their own beer descriptions with a chatbot.
fieldNote: Grace's job and **savings** feel secure here; her worries are about client cash flow.
She thinks first of **Lena**, the copywriter, whose work is more exposed.
Her favourite part of the job, **press checks**, is hands-on and physical.

steps.text: Keep mocking up beer cans with the image tool and attending press checks
Raise her pension contributions now the worst case looks unlikely

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to talk about this as a team, before Marcus decides on his own. Online I'd back calls for rules on AI in creative work and for help for people who lose out. I'd probably say the agency should share the time it saves, maybe with a four-day week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the agency shrinks and I could be part of that. Planning, checking proofs, writing to clients and first designs are a big part of my day, and software could take a lot of it. Nine people could become six, and I'm average at this job, not a star.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools more seriously, but carefully, maybe two afternoons a month testing what they can actually do for packaging. I'd ask Marcus for more of the press-check and client-visit work, because that's the part software doesn't do well. And I'd quietly look at in-house design jobs at bigger food firms, where there might be more security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a knot that tightens when Marcus closes his office door. I'd feel like I was auditioning for my own job every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tools carefully. What does careful mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't feed clients' unreleased label designs into some public tool. A brewery's new beer is a secret until launch day. I'd only use what the agency has a proper licence for, and I'd ask what happens to the files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost the job, what would that mean for you and Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be okay for eight months, and Tom fixes buses, which isn't going anywhere soon. But we'd been planning to stop renting and buy somewhere, and that would go on hold. I'd hate being the reason we wait.

say: The team should **talk together** before Marcus decides alone.
The agency should **share the time saved**, perhaps with a four-day week.
think: **Nine people** could become six, and I'm average, not a star.
Proofs, client emails and first drafts are the **thinking work** software takes first.
do: Test AI tools for packaging on **two afternoons** a month, with licensed software only.
Ask Marcus for more **press checks** and client visits.
Look at **in-house design jobs** at bigger food firms.
feel: A **knot** that tightens when Marcus closes his office door.
Like **auditioning** for my own job every week.
S1.quote: Nine people could become six, and I'm average at this job, not a star.
fieldNote: Grace is **honest about her skill**, which sharpens her worry about cuts.
She shifts toward the **hands-on** parts of the job: press checks and client visits.
Her care about **client secrets** shapes how she'd use AI tools.

steps.text: Test licensed AI packaging tools on two afternoons a month
Ask Marcus to give her more press checks and client visits
Apply for in-house design jobs at larger food companies
Put the plan to buy a flat with Tom on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to cope with and the government has to step in. I'd sign every petition for a basic income or wage support. At work I think we'd all be in a kind of shock, talking about it at every lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd expect to lose my job within a year or two of it arriving. Branding a beer is almost all thinking work, and if a machine does it as well and cheaper, Marcus can't compete by keeping nine humans. The press checks give me a little longer, maybe the three years until robots, but that's not a whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything big and get the savings from eight months to as close to a year as I could. I'd look hard at work that's mostly hands-on, like working at the label printer itself, because they'd still need people for a few years. And I'd join whatever union or group was pushing for wage support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Every time I picture losing my packaging job, I go cold, because AGI in two years is not a slow change I can steer, it's a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning change for you, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I couldn't retrain into something properly, like teaching or a trade. I'd have to grab something close by, like press work, and hope it buys time. The slower pictures at least let me choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, that same evening, probably at the kitchen table with the laptop open on our bank account. Then my mum, who worked in a print shop for years and would actually understand what press work is like.

say: This is **too fast** to cope with, and the government must step in.
I'd sign every petition for **wage support** or a basic income.
think: I'd expect to **lose my job** within a year or two of AGI arriving.
**Press checks** might give me three more years, but not a whole job.
do: Stop **big spending** and push savings toward a full year.
Apply for **hands-on work** at the label printer.
Join a **union or group** pushing for wage support.
feel: **Scared**, and cold, because this feels like a **cliff** rather than a slope.
S2.quote: Every time I picture losing my packaging job, I go cold, because AGI in two years is not a slow change I can steer, it's a cliff.
fieldNote: Grace expects to **lose her job** and sees press work only as a few extra years.
The **two-year warning** rules out retraining; she'd grab whatever is nearest.
She'd turn to **Tom and her mum**, who knows print shop work.

steps.text: Push savings from eight months to a full year of costs
Apply for press work at the label printer the agency uses
Join a union pushing for wage support for designers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years and we should use them, so let's push for retraining money now. At the agency I'd suggest we all sit down with Marcus and make a plan instead of pretending. Online I'd share anything useful about courses and grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think my job ends, but five years means I could be somewhere else by then. I'd be thirty-two when AGI arrives, which is a good age to have switched. The question is to what, because a lot of desk jobs go at the same time as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in occupational therapy, because it's hands-on, it helps people, and it's not all screen work. I'd keep working at the agency and use AI tools a bit more to stay useful while I study. I'd keep saving at the same rate so the switch doesn't wipe us out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable but not panicky. It's like knowing a flat you love will be sold in a few years; you start looking before you're forced to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why occupational therapy? It's quite a jump from beer labels.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt had a stroke two years ago, and the therapist who helped her get back to cooking was brilliant. It's practical, it's with people, and the paperwork part is the only bit AI would take. It feels like a job where a person in the room still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that plan feel realistic, or more like a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere in between. It's three years of study and I'd take a pay cut at the start. With five years' warning and good savings, switching to occupational therapy is the first time this feels like a choice rather than a panic.

say: We have **a few years**, so let's push for retraining money now.
The agency should make **a real plan** with Marcus instead of pretending.
think: My job **still ends**, but I could be somewhere else by then.
I'd be **thirty-two** at AGI, a good age to have switched careers.

Use **AI tools** a bit more at work to stay useful while I study.

feel: **Uncomfortable** but not panicky, like a loved flat being sold in a few years.
S3.quote: With five years' warning and good savings, switching to occupational therapy is the first time this feels like a choice rather than a panic.
fieldNote: Grace's **career switch** comes from a real memory: her aunt's stroke therapist.
She expects her **design job** to end, but feels some control with five years.
She would keep **using AI** at work as a bridge, not a future.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening occupational therapy course in the first year
Use the agency's AI tools more to stay useful while studying
Keep saving at the same monthly rate to fund the switch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly, and we should demand that governments use it. Shorter weeks, retraining support, shared gains from the companies. At the agency I'd say let's enjoy the work we have while helping each other plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the end of this job, but it's slow enough that I'd probably be fine. Ten years is a long time in a career; I could get the therapy qualification and work in it for years before robots reach hands-on care around 2039. The scary part is less about me and more about whether everyone else gets help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I wouldn't quit anything. I'd keep designing, use the tools where they help, and maybe take one evening class to test whether therapy is really for me. I'd also keep active in a designers' group so we push for the support together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's room to breathe. It feels like a long road with a known bend, not a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. Is that the money, or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the time. The savings help, but it's the decade that matters, because I can try something, fail and try again. Tom keeps saying I worry ahead of time, and in this picture he'd probably be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope to have done by the time AGI arrives in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope to be a qualified therapist, maybe with a part-time design client or two for fun. I'd like to be thirty-seven with a house and a job where people need me in the room. That doesn't sound too much to ask with ten years.

say: Ten years is enough to **do it properly**, so governments must use it.
We need **shorter weeks**, retraining support and shared gains from AI firms.
think: The design job still ends, but **the decade** gives me time to switch well.
My bigger worry is whether **everyone else** gets help.
do: Keep **designing** in year one and use the tools where they help.
Take **one evening class** to test whether therapy suits me.
Stay active in a **designers' group** pushing for support.
feel: **Uneasy** but with room to breathe, like a road with a **known bend**.
S4.quote: I'd like to be thirty-seven with a house and a job where people need me in the room.
fieldNote: With ten years, Grace's fear turns into **trial and error**: she can test therapy first.
Her design **income still goes**, but she feels largely in control.
Her politics stay focused on **others**: shorter weeks and shared gains.

steps.text: Keep designing beer labels at the agency through the first year
Take one evening class to test whether occupational therapy suits her
Stay active in a designers' group pushing for retraining support

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's a cliff and not a slope. What would help most is wage support while people retrain, and free or cheap courses for jobs like therapy or care that need people in the room. And honestly, agencies like ours sharing the savings with staff instead of just cutting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd keep doing for love. Even if no one paid me, I'd still draw beer labels for friends who brew at home. A machine taking my job doesn't take away that I like making things.

headlineQuote: Standing next to a huge machine with a cup of bad coffee, holding a wet label up to the light, is the best bit of the job.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old** packaging designer at a nine-person agency for breweries and bakeries.
She uses AI **now and then** and guards client secrets carefully.
Her **press checks** are the hands-on part she loves and the last part software reaches.
From Steady Disruption on she expects her **job to end**, and plans a move into occupational therapy.
She wants **wage support**, retraining help and agencies sharing savings with staff.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years feels like a cliff rather than a slope.
whatWouldHelp: **Wage support** while retraining and cheap courses for people-centred jobs like therapy.
Agencies **sharing the savings** with staff instead of only cutting jobs.
